chapters.title: Chapter 5: GST Basics for Business Owners

lessons.title: How GST Works: Output Tax, Input Tax Credit and the Supply Chain

body.text: GST is not a tax on your business. It is a tax on your customer that passes through your business, and you only ever hand over the tax on the value you added. The entire system rests on that one idea, and every GST problem a business has is the chain breaking somewhere.

children.text: Income tax arrives once a year and is computed by your accountant. GST arrives every month, is computed by your billing system, and touches every invoice your business raises or receives. For most owners it is the tax they actually feel, and it is the one where a supplier's mistake becomes your cost.

body.latex: \text{GST payable in cash} = \text{Output tax on sales} - \text{Input tax credit on purchases}
body.caption: Collect on what you sell, offset what you paid, remit the difference

children.text: The Chain, Followed End to End
Take a product taxed at 18%, moving from a raw material supplier through a manufacturer and a wholesaler to a retailer in Maharashtra, and finally to a customer who walks in off the street.

body.caption: Who pays what at each stage, at 18%

body.title: Cash actually remitted at each stage, adding up to ₹28,800

body.text: Read the last column and then the total. Four businesses remitted ₹28,800 between them, which is exactly the 18% the final customer paid on ₹1,60,000. Nobody in the chain bore the tax, and nobody paid tax on tax. Each business paid only on the value it added, which is why the old system of tax on tax was worth replacing.

body.title: Where the invoice goes decides which tax you charge

columns.label: Within the same state
points: The central half goes to the Centre and the state half to that state
Your invoice must show both lines separately
A Pune seller billing a Pune buyer

columns.label: Across state lines
points: The full 18% is charged as IGST
Collected centrally and settled with the destination state
One line on the invoice instead of two
A Pune seller billing a Bengaluru buyer

body.text: Getting this split wrong is the most common GST invoicing error and it is genuinely painful to fix. Charging CGST and SGST on what was actually an inter-state supply means your customer cannot claim the credit, you have paid the wrong governments, and correcting it means credit notes, amended returns and a refund claim. The deciding factor is the place of supply, which for goods is usually where they are delivered.

body.title: What the September 2025 rate reform changed

children.text: GST launched in 2017 with four main slabs of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%, plus a cess on some goods. Classification disputes followed, because a small difference in description could move a product between slabs.

From 22 September 2025, the GST Council largely removed the 12% and 28% slabs. Most 12% items moved down to 5% or up to 18%, and most 28% items came down to 18%, while a new 40% rate was created for tobacco, pan masala and selected luxury goods. For a business, the practical consequence is that rate masters in billing software, price lists and contracts all needed updating, and older invoices in your files will show rates that no longer exist.

markDefs.definition: The auto-generated monthly statement of input tax credit available to a buyer, built from the invoices that suppliers have reported in their own GST returns.

children.text: Paying GST to your supplier is not enough to claim credit for it. Five conditions have to hold, and the hardest one is outside your control: the invoice has to appear in your
, which only happens if your supplier has reported it.

body.caption: The five conditions for claiming input tax credit

cells: You hold a valid tax invoice
Missing GSTIN, wrong address, or a proforma invoice filed as a tax invoice
You have actually received the goods or services
Credit claimed on advance payment before delivery
The invoice appears in your GSTR-2B
Supplier files late, files wrong, or does not file at all
The tax has reached the government
Supplier collects the tax from you and never deposits it
You pay the supplier within 180 days
Long credit terms quietly reverse the credit you already took

body.title: Try It: What Goes Out in Cash
body.prompt: In a month, a business raises sales invoices of ₹40,00,000 plus GST at 18%. Its purchases eligible for credit are ₹25,00,000 plus GST at 18%, and every one of those invoices appears in its GSTR-2B. How much GST must it pay in cash? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Output tax is 18% of ₹40,00,000, which is ₹7,20,000. Input tax credit is 18% of ₹25,00,000, which is ₹4,50,000. The difference of ₹2,70,000 is paid in cash. Notice that this equals 18% of the ₹15,00,000 of value the business added, which is the whole design of the tax.

children.text: Credits You Cannot Claim at All
Some purchases are blocked by law, however genuinely they are used in the business. For these, GST is a straight cost and belongs in your budget as one.

cells: Motor cars for employee or director use
Blocked, with exceptions for transport businesses, driving schools and dealers
Food, beverages, outdoor catering and staff refreshments
Blocked, unless you are in the same line of business or the law obliges you to provide it
Construction of an immovable property on your own account
Blocked, even when the building is used for the business
Goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or given as free samples
Blocked, and any credit already taken must be reversed

body.title: Quick Check: Which Credit Survives?
body.question: A manufacturing company buys four things this month. On which one can it claim input tax credit?
options: A car for the managing director's use
A new shed constructed on its own factory land
Raw materials from a supplier who has filed the invoice correctly
A corporate gym membership for senior staff
body.explanation: Only the raw materials. Motor cars, construction of immovable property on your own account and club or fitness memberships are all blocked, whatever the business rationale. The raw material credit works because the purchase is used in the business and, critically, the supplier reported the invoice so it appears in GSTR-2B.

body.title: Scenario: The Supplier Who Stopped Filing
body.scenario: A Bengaluru electronics assembler buys ₹60,00,000 of components a year from one vendor, with GST of ₹10,80,000 at 18%. Every invoice is genuine, every payment went by bank transfer, and the goods are on the shop floor. At the half-year review, the finance team finds that ₹4,20,000 of that GST is missing from GSTR-2B, because the vendor has not filed its returns for four months.
body.prompt: What is the company's position, and what should it do?
body.modelAnswer: The credit is not available while the invoices sit outside GSTR-2B, however honest the transaction was. That ₹4,20,000 becomes cash the company must pay to the government on top of what it has already paid its vendor, so it is a working capital hit first and a potential permanent cost if never resolved. Four steps follow. Chase the vendor immediately and in writing, because only the vendor can file and fix this, and be specific about the invoices and periods involved. Hold back further payments where the contract allows, since paying a supplier who is not remitting your tax funds the problem. Check whether a GST clause exists in the purchase agreement making the vendor liable for credit lost through its non-compliance, and add one for the future if not. Then reconcile GSTR-2B against the purchase ledger every month rather than every six, because four months of drift is what turned an irritation into ₹4,20,000. If the vendor has genuinely gone under, take professional advice on the claim, but plan the cash flow on the assumption that the credit is gone. Vendor GST compliance is a procurement criterion, not an accounting afterthought.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Payment Clock
body.textWithBlank: Input tax credit already claimed must be reversed if the supplier is not paid within ___ days of the invoice date.
body.explanation: One hundred and eighty days. The credit can be reclaimed once payment is finally made, so it is a timing problem rather than a permanent loss, but it catches businesses that negotiate long credit terms and then forget the GST consequence of their own payment policy.

body.label: Why GST ends up costing you money
body.context: For a registered business making taxable supplies, GST should be cash flow, not cost. It becomes a real cost only through blocked credits, suppliers who do not file, exempt output supplies, and credits reversed for late payment.

body.text: There is one more way the chain runs backwards. Under reverse charge, the buyer pays the tax instead of the seller, which applies to certain notified supplies and to most purchases from unregistered persons in specified cases. The buyer pays the tax in cash and then claims it as credit if otherwise eligible, so the paperwork matters more than the money.

body.title: Monthly Input Tax Credit Hygiene
steps: Download GSTR-2B and reconcile it against the purchase ledger every single month, without exception
List the invoices missing from GSTR-2B and chase those suppliers within the same week
Flag purchases in blocked categories at the time of booking, so the GST goes to expense rather than to credit
Track invoices approaching 180 days unpaid and either pay them or plan the reversal
Check that every sales invoice carries the right split of CGST and SGST or IGST, based on place of supply
Confirm your billing software's rate master reflects the current slabs after the 2025 reform
Keep a GST compliance clause in vendor contracts, making the supplier answerable for credit lost through its default

cards.definition: The GST you charge your customers on sales and are liable to remit.
The GST you paid on business purchases, offset against output tax so you pay only on the value you added.
The two halves of GST on a supply within one state, going to the Centre and that state.
The single tax charged on an inter-state supply, collected centrally and settled with the destination state.
The rule that decides which state the supply belongs to, and therefore whether you charge CGST and SGST or IGST.
The auto-generated statement of credit available to you, built from what your suppliers have reported.
GST on specified purchases, such as cars and club memberships, that can never be claimed as credit.
Cases where the buyer, not the seller, is liable to pay the GST to the government.

points: GST is collected at every stage but borne only by the final customer, because each business offsets the tax on its purchases
You remit output tax on sales less input tax credit on purchases, so you pay only on the value you added
A supply within a state carries CGST and SGST, while an inter-state supply carries IGST, decided by place of supply
Since 22 September 2025 the main slabs are 0%, 5%, 18% and 40%, with 12% and 28% largely removed
Credit requires a valid invoice, actual receipt, the invoice appearing in GSTR-2B, tax reaching the government, and payment to the supplier within 180 days
Cars, food and beverages, club memberships and own-account construction are blocked credits and are a real cost
Your supplier's compliance decides your credit, which makes vendor selection a tax decision

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. GST rates, slabs, credit conditions and exceptions are set under the GST laws and change through GST Council decisions and notifications, including the significant rate reform of September 2025. Classification of a specific product or service can be genuinely difficult. Confirm the current position with a qualified GST practitioner before applying any of this to your own invoices.
